
# How to Recognize Common Text Message Scams: Complete Beginner's Guide


## What is this in plain English?


Remember when scams meant someone literally knocking on your door pretending to sell something, or calling on your landline phone during dinner with a too-good-to-be-true offer? You could hear their voice, judge their credibility, hang up if suspicious, and tell them never to call again. The scammer had to actually interact with you in real-time, making scams labor-intensive and limited in scale. A con artist could only contact a handful of people per day, and most people developed healthy skepticism toward unexpected sales pitches.


Text message scams—often called "smishing" (SMS + phishing)—changed everything. A scammer sitting anywhere in the world can send millions of text messages simultaneously at virtually no cost, pretending to be your bank, Amazon, the post office, the IRS, your phone company, or even your own family member. The messages create urgency ("Your account will be locked!"), fear ("Suspicious activity detected!"), or curiosity ("Your package couldn't be delivered") to make you click a link or reply with personal information before thinking carefully. Unlike phone calls where you can hear a suspicious accent or unprofessional background noise, text messages look official, use company logos, and seem to come from legitimate phone numbers.


The scale is staggering: Americans receive an estimated 11 billion scam text messages annually. That's roughly 44,000 scam texts every minute, 24 hours a day. Most get caught by phone carrier filters, but enough slip through that nearly everyone receives several per month. The financial impact is equally stunning—consumers lost over $330 million to text message scams in 2022 alone, and that's only reported losses. The actual number is likely far higher since many victims don't report out of embarrassment.


This guide teaches you to recognize text message scams instantly, understand the psychological tactics scammers use, identify the specific red flags that reveal a scam, know what to do when you receive a suspicious text (and what not to do), protect yourself from these scams, report them to help others, and understand why these scams work so you can resist the manipulation. Whether you've never fallen for a scam or you've been victimized before, this guide gives you the knowledge to protect yourself and your family.


The good news: text message scams follow predictable patterns. Once you know what to look for, they become obvious—like seeing a magic trick explained. You'll wonder how you ever found them convincing.


## Before You Start: Understanding Text Message Scams


**What Are Text Message Scams (Smishing)?**


**Smishing** = SMS (text messaging) + Phishing (fraudulent attempts to obtain sensitive information)


Scammers send text messages pretending to be legitimate organizations to:

1. Steal personal information (passwords, Social Security numbers, bank details)
2. Steal money directly (through fake payments or gift card requests)
3. Install malware on your phone (through malicious links)
4. Gain access to your accounts (by getting you to reveal login credentials)

**Why Text Messages Instead of Email or Phone Calls?**


**Scammers prefer texts because:**

- **Higher open rate:** 98% of texts are opened (vs. 20% of emails)
- **Faster response:** People read texts within 3 minutes on average
- **More trusted:** People assume texts come from real people/companies
- **Harder to verify:** Can't hear suspicious voice or check email headers
- **Mobile urgency:** Reading on phone encourages quick, impulsive responses
- **No spam filters:** Until recently, text spam filters were poor (improving now)
- **Cheap and easy:** Sending millions of texts costs almost nothing

**How Scammers Get Your Number:**


You may wonder: "How did they get MY number?"


**Common sources:**

- **Data breaches:** Your number leaked from hacked companies (stored in databases)
- **Public records:** Phone numbers in public databases, voter registrations, property records
- **Social media:** Phone number visible on Facebook, LinkedIn, or other platforms
- **Random generation:** Computers generate millions of phone numbers automatically
- **Previous scams:** Once you respond to one scam, your number marked as "active" (gets sold to other scammers)
- **"Free" services:** Entering number to win contests, get coupons, claim prizes

**Your number being targeted doesn't mean you did anything wrong**—most numbers eventually get scammed.


**The Psychology Behind Text Scams:**


Scammers exploit human psychology deliberately:


**1. Urgency:**

- "Act within 24 hours or account will be closed"
- "Immediate action required"
- Creates panic, bypasses rational thinking

**2. Fear:**

- "Suspicious activity detected"
- "Your account has been compromised"
- "Legal action will be taken"
- Fear makes people react without thinking

**3. Authority:**

- Pretending to be bank, government, well-known company
- People tend to obey perceived authority

**4. Curiosity:**

- "Your package couldn't be delivered"
- "You've won a prize"
- "Someone sent you money"
- Curiosity makes you click to find out more

**5. Greed:**

- "Claim your refund"
- "You're eligible for $1,200"
- Too good to be true, but greed clouds judgment

**6. Social proof/trust:**

- "Dear valued customer" (implies you have relationship)
- Using real company names and logos
- Exploits trust in familiar brands

**Understanding these tactics makes you resistant to them.**


**Common Types of Text Message Scams:**


**Package delivery scams:**

- "Your package couldn't be delivered. Click here to reschedule."
- "USPS: Parcel is waiting. Confirm shipping address."
- Exploits fact that many people order online frequently

**Bank/financial scams:**

- "Your [Bank Name] account has been locked. Verify identity immediately."
- "Unusual activity detected on your account. Click to secure."
- Creates fear, demands immediate action

**Government impersonation:**

- "IRS: You have unclaimed tax refund of $847. Claim here."
- "Social Security: Your number has been suspended due to suspicious activity."
- Uses authority of government to intimidate

**Prize/lottery scams:**

- "Congratulations! You've won $5,000. Claim your prize."
- "You've been selected for a Walmart gift card. Click here."
- Exploits greed and excitement

**Tech support scams:**

- "Apple: Your iCloud storage is full. Upgrade now."
- "Microsoft: Your computer has a virus. Click to fix."
- Creates technical anxiety

**Family emergency scams:**

- "Mom, I lost my phone. This is my new number. Need money urgently."
- "Hey, it's me. My phone broke. Can you send $500?"
- Exploits emotional bonds and desire to help family

**Romance/dating scams:**

- Messages from "attractive" strangers wanting to connect
- Eventually ask for money, gift cards, or personal info
- Long-term manipulation

**Job offer scams:**

- "You've been selected for work-from-home job paying $5,000/month."
- Asks for personal info "for background check" or upfront fees

**Two-factor authentication (2FA) code fishing:**

- "Your verification code is 482901. Reply if you didn't request this."
- Tricks you into giving 2FA code they requested (to hack your account)

## Step 1: Universal Red Flags (Applies to ALL Scam Texts)


**These warning signs appear in nearly every scam text. If you see ANY of these, be immediately suspicious:**


**Red Flag 1: Unsolicited Contact**


**If you didn't initiate the conversation, be skeptical.**

- ✅ Legitimate: You ordered package, expect delivery text
- ❌ Scam: Random text about package you didn't order
- ✅ Legitimate: You contacted bank, they text back
- ❌ Scam: Unexpected text from "bank" about problem

**Companies rarely text you out of the blue about urgent problems.**


**Red Flag 2: Urgent or Threatening Language**


**Scammers create false urgency to bypass critical thinking.**


**Urgent phrases that scream "scam":**

- "Immediate action required"
- "Within 24 hours or account will be closed"
- "Respond now to avoid legal action"
- "Your account will be suspended unless..."
- "Act immediately"
- "Last chance"
- "Time-sensitive"

**Legitimate companies:**

- Give you reasonable time to respond (days or weeks, not hours)
- Don't threaten account closure via text
- Send multiple notices before taking action
- Don't create artificial panic

**Red Flag 3: Requests for Personal Information**


**Legitimate companies NEVER ask for sensitive info via text.**


**Never provide via text:**

- ❌ Social Security Number
- ❌ Bank account numbers
- ❌ Credit card numbers (full number, especially)
- ❌ Passwords or PINs
- ❌ Mother's maiden name
- ❌ Date of birth
- ❌ Two-factor authentication codes

**If text asks for any of these = 100% scam.**


**Red Flag 4: Suspicious Links**


**Scam texts almost always include a link.**


**What to look for:**


**Shortened links:**

- bit.ly/x7k9m2 (hides real destination)
- tinyurl.com/abc123
- Can't see where it actually goes

**Misspelled domains:**

- amaz0n.com (zero instead of 'o')
- paypa1.com (number 1 instead of letter 'l')
- chase-secure.com (real Chase is chase.com)
- wellsfarg0.com
- netfl1x.com

**Suspicious domains:**

- random-letters.com (gibberish domains)
- .tk, .xyz, .club extensions (commonly used by scammers)
- IP addresses instead of domain names ([http://192.168.x.x](http://192.168.x.x/))

**Legitimate companies:**

- Use their official domain (amazon.com, usps.com, chase.com)
- Don't use link shorteners for important communications
- Have consistent URLs across all communications

**How to check a link without clicking:**

- Long-press link (mobile) → Preview shows actual destination URL
- Don't click if anything seems off

**Red Flag 5: Generic Greetings**


**Scammers don't know your name.**


**Scam greetings:**

- "Dear customer"
- "Valued member"
- "Dear account holder"
- "Hello user"
- No greeting at all, just jumps into message

**Legitimate companies:**

- Usually use your actual name: "Hello John Smith"
- Have your name in their database (you're a customer)

**Exception:** Some legitimate automated texts use generic greetings, but combined with other red flags, it's suspicious.


**Red Flag 6: Grammar and Spelling Errors**


**Professional companies proofread communications.**


**Common errors in scams:**

- "You're account has been compromised" (your, not you're)
- "Click here for confirming you're identity"
- Random capitalization
- Missing punctuation or excessive punctuation!!!
- Awkward phrasing (often from poor translation)

**Recent trend:** Some scams now have perfect grammar (use AI or hire native speakers), so this alone isn't reliable—but obvious errors are still a strong indicator.


**Red Flag 7: Requests for Immediate Payment (Especially Gift Cards)**


**No legitimate company or government agency accepts payment via:**

- Gift cards (Google Play, Apple, Amazon, iTunes, prepaid Visa)
- Cryptocurrency (Bitcoin, etc.)
- Wire transfer (Western Union, MoneyGram)
- Cash apps (Zelle, Venmo, CashApp for strangers)

**If text demands payment in any of these forms = definitely scam.**


**Why scammers love gift cards:**

- Untraceable (unlike credit cards or checks)
- Irreversible (can't dispute like credit card charges)
- Easy to redeem (drain value within minutes)
- Victim realizes scam too late

**Legitimate companies accept:**

- Credit cards (official website or over phone)
- Checks mailed to official address
- Direct bank payments (on official website or app)

**Red Flag 8: Too Good to Be True**


**If it sounds impossibly good, it is.**


**Examples:**

- "You've won $5,000!" (you didn't enter any contest)
- "Claim your $1,200 stimulus check" (sent randomly, not from IRS)
- "Free iPhone 15! Click to claim" (nothing is free)
- "Make $10,000/month working from home, no experience needed"

**Reality check:** Why would a stranger give you free money? They wouldn't.


**Red Flag 9: Mismatched Sender Information**


**Text claims to be from one company but sender info doesn't match.**


**What to check:**


**Sender phone number:**

- Legitimate companies often use short codes (5-6 digit numbers) or recognizable numbers
- Random 10-digit numbers claiming to be major companies = suspicious
- International numbers (+44, +91, etc.) claiming to be US companies = scam

**Sender name:**

- Phone may display "USPS" or "Bank Name" based on contact info scammers provide
- This can be spoofed (faked)—don't trust sender name alone

**Content vs. claimed identity:**

- Text says "from Amazon" but sent from random number
- Claims to be bank but uses generic email or informal language

**Red Flag 10: Unusual Requests from "Family or Friends"**


**Scammers impersonate people you know.**


**Signs of impersonation:**

- "Hey, this is my new number" (then asks for money)
- "Can you send me $500? I'll explain later"
- Different texting style than usual
- Unusual requests (family member who never asks for money suddenly needs $1,000)
- Urgency: "Need it NOW, don't call, just send"

**What to do:**

- Call the person on their known number (not the number that texted you)
- Ask question only real person would know
- Verify via different communication channel (Facebook Messenger, email)

**Scammers count on you not verifying.**


## Step 2: Specific Scam Categories and How to Recognize Them


**Package Delivery Scams:**


**What they look like:**


"USPS: Your package is waiting for delivery. Confirm shipping address: [link]"


"FedEx: We attempted delivery but no one was home. Reschedule here: [link]"


"DHL: Parcel held due to incomplete address. Update info: [link]"


**How to recognize:**

- ❌ You didn't order anything recently (or you did, but tracking info doesn't match)
- ❌ Real USPS/FedEx/UPS don't text from random numbers
- ❌ Link goes to suspicious domain (usps-delivery.com instead of usps.com)
- ❌ Asks for payment to release package (real carriers bill shipper, not recipient)
- ❌ Asks for personal info (SSN, card number) to "confirm identity"

**What scammers want:**

- Personal information (name, address, payment info)
- Payment ($1-3 "redelivery fee" is phishing for card number)
- Install malware (clicking link downloads virus)

**How to verify:**

- Check tracking number on official carrier website (usps.com, fedex.com, ups.com)
- Check email for legitimate tracking notifications
- Contact carrier directly via official website or phone number

**Bank/Financial Scams:**


**What they look like:**


"Bank of America: Your account has been locked due to suspicious activity. Verify identity immediately: [link]"


"Chase Alert: Unusual transaction of $847.23 detected. If this wasn't you, click here."


"Venmo: Your account will be suspended. Update payment information: [link]"


**How to recognize:**

- ❌ Real banks don't text links for account issues (they tell you to call or visit bank)
- ❌ Creates urgency ("locked," "suspended," "immediate")
- ❌ Link goes to fake bank website (chase-secure.com, not chase.com)
- ❌ Asks for full account number, SSN, or password

**What scammers want:**

- Login credentials (username and password)
- Account numbers and routing numbers
- Debit card number, CVV, PIN
- Access to drain account

**How to verify:**

- **Never click link in text**
- Open banking app or go to bank's website directly (type URL yourself)
- Log in—check for actual alerts
- Call bank using number on back of card (not number in text)

**Government Impersonation Scams:**


**What they look like:**


"IRS: You are eligible for tax refund of $1,247. Claim here: [link]"


"Social Security Administration: Your SSN has been suspended due to suspicious activity. Call 888-xxx-xxxx immediately."


"Medicare: Your benefits will be terminated unless you verify information."


**How to recognize:**

- ❌ IRS doesn't text about refunds (sends physical letters)
- ❌ Social Security numbers can't be "suspended"
- ❌ Government agencies don't demand immediate action via text
- ❌ Asks for SSN, payment, or personal info via text
- ❌ Threatens arrest or legal action

**What scammers want:**

- Social Security Number
- Bank account info ("for direct deposit of refund")
- Payment (for fake fees, fines, or to "reactivate" benefits)

**How to verify:**

- Visit official government website (irs.gov, ssa.gov)
- Call official number (look it up yourself—don't use number in text)
- IRS first contact is always by mail (never text, email, or social media)

**Prize/Sweepstakes Scams:**


**What they look like:**


"Congratulations! You've been selected to receive a $500 Walmart gift card. Claim now: [link]"


"You've won! Click here to claim your prize before it expires."


"Amazon is giving away free iPhones to celebrate Prime Day. Get yours: [link]"


**How to recognize:**

- ❌ You didn't enter any contest or sweepstakes
- ❌ Real sweepstakes notify winners by mail or phone (with official verification)
- ❌ Asks for payment to "claim" prize (shipping fee, taxes, processing)
- ❌ Asks for bank info "to deposit winnings"
- ❌ Creates urgency ("expires in 24 hours")

**Reality:** You can't win a contest you didn't enter. Major companies don't give away prizes via random texts.


**What scammers want:**

- Payment ("shipping fee," "taxes")
- Personal information (for "verification" or "prize delivery")
- Credit card number

**Tech Support / Account Security Scams:**


**What they look like:**


"Apple: Your iCloud account has been compromised. Secure your account: [link]"


"Microsoft: Your Windows license has expired. Renew now to avoid data loss."


"Netflix: Your subscription has been cancelled due to billing issue. Update payment: [link]"


**How to recognize:**

- ❌ Real tech companies don't text about account issues
- ❌ Link goes to fake domain (apple-security.com, not apple.com)
- ❌ Microsoft doesn't text about Windows licenses
- ❌ Netflix emails about billing issues (doesn't text)

**What scammers want:**

- Account login credentials
- Credit card information
- Install malware ("click here to scan for viruses")

**How to verify:**

- Open app directly (Netflix app, iCloud settings)
- Check for actual alerts or issues
- Visit official website by typing URL yourself

**Family Emergency / Impersonation Scams:**


**What they look like:**


"Hi Mom, I lost my phone. This is my new number. Can you send $300 for emergency? I'll explain later."


"Hey, it's me. Phone broke, using friend's phone. Need money for repair. Venmo me at [number]."


"Grandma, I'm in trouble. Need bail money. Please don't tell mom. Send $2,000 to [account]."


**How to recognize:**

- ❌ Unusual request from family member
- ❌ Urgency ("need money NOW")
- ❌ Asks you not to verify with others
- ❌ Different communication style than usual
- ❌ Explanation seems vague or doesn't make sense

**What scammers want:**

- Money via wire transfer, Zelle, Venmo, gift cards
- Emotional urgency prevents you from thinking clearly

**How to verify:**

- **Call the person on their known number** (not the number that texted)
- Ask question only real person would know ("What's my dog's name?" "Where did we have dinner last week?")
- Contact another family member to verify
- Take time to think—emergencies can wait 10 minutes for verification

**Scammers exploit your love for family.**


**Romance / Dating Scams:**


**What they look like:**


"Hi! You seem interesting. I'd love to get to know you. Here's my photo: [link]"


Prolonged conversation building trust, then: "I need money for emergency. Can you help?"


**How to recognize:**

- ❌ Unsolicited romantic interest from stranger
- ❌ Attractive photos (often stolen from internet)
- ❌ Quickly professes strong feelings
- ❌ Eventually asks for money (medical emergency, travel to meet you, investment opportunity)
- ❌ Avoids video calls (excuses: broken camera, poor internet)

**What scammers want:**

- Money (the real goal)
- Personal information
- Long-term manipulation

**Timeline:** Can take weeks or months building trust before asking for money.


## Step 3: What to Do When You Receive a Suspicious Text


**Follow this exact process—it protects you from nearly all scams:**


**Step 1: Don't Panic**


**Scammers want you panicked and reacting impulsively.**

- Take a breath
- Remind yourself: "This is probably a scam"
- Don't act immediately

**Step 2: Don't Click Any Links**


**The link is the trap.**

- **Never click links in suspicious texts**
- Even "just to see where it goes"
- Links can install malware just by visiting
- Or steal information when you enter it

**Step 3: Don't Reply**


**Replying confirms your number is active.**

- Don't reply "STOP"
- Don't reply "Who is this?"
- Don't engage in any way
- Replying tells scammers: "This number is real and monitored—send more scams"

**Step 4: Don't Call Any Phone Numbers in the Text**


**Phone numbers in scam texts go to scammers, not legitimate companies.**

- Don't call numbers in the text
- Look up official number yourself (Google the company, find official website)
- Call that official number if you need to verify

**Step 5: Verify Independently**


**If text claims to be from a company you actually do business with:**


**For banks:**

1. Open banking app (don't click link in text)
2. Check for alerts or notifications
3. OR call number on back of your debit/credit card
4. Ask: "Did you text me about [issue]?"

**For package deliveries:**

1. Check email for tracking notifications
2. OR visit carrier's official website (usps.com, fedex.com)
3. Enter tracking number manually
4. See if package exists and status

**For other companies:**

1. Visit official website (type URL yourself)
2. Log into your account
3. Check for actual alerts or messages
4. OR call customer service via number on official website

**For government agencies:**

1. Visit official website (.gov domains)
2. Call official number listed on website
3. Ask if they contacted you

**Step 6: Look for Red Flags**


**Review the text against red flags in Steps 1 and 2:**

- Unsolicited contact?
- Urgent or threatening?
- Asks for personal info?
- Suspicious link?
- Too good to be true?
- Generic greeting?
- Grammar errors?
- Requests gift card payment?

**If ANY red flags present: It's a scam.**


**Step 7: Delete the Text**


**Once determined to be scam:**

- Delete the text
- Block the number (prevents future texts from that number)
    - iPhone: Tap number → Info (i) → Block this Caller
    - Android: Tap number → Details → Block & report spam

**Step 8: Report the Scam**


**Help protect others:**


**Forward to 7726 (SPAM):**

- Works on all carriers (AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, etc.)
- Free to send
- Carrier investigates and blocks number

**Report to FTC:**

- Visit reportfraud.ftc.gov
- File complaint
- Helps authorities track scam trends

**Report to company being impersonated:**

- Many companies have scam reporting email
- Examples:
    - Amazon: [stop-spoofing@amazon.com](mailto:stop-spoofing@amazon.com)
    - IRS: [phishing@irs.gov](mailto:phishing@irs.gov)
    - USPS: [spam@uspis.gov](mailto:spam@uspis.gov)

**Step 9: Warn Others**


**Tell friends and family, especially:**

- Elderly relatives (frequently targeted)
- Younger family members (less experience with scams)
- Anyone you know who might fall for it

**Share knowledge, not shame.** Many smart people fall for sophisticated scams.


## Step 4: What NOT to Do


**These actions make the problem worse:**


**DON'T Reply "STOP"**


**Many believe replying "STOP" unsubscribes from scam texts. It doesn't.**

- "STOP" works for legitimate marketing texts
- For scammers, it confirms: "This number is active"
- Results in more scam texts, not fewer
- Scammers sell "confirmed active" numbers to other scammers

**Correct action:** Delete and block, don't reply at all.


**DON'T Click the Link (Even Out of Curiosity)**


**"I'll just see where it goes" is dangerous.**

- Malicious links can install malware just by clicking
- Fake websites steal information when you enter it
- Some links track that you clicked (confirms active number)

**Even tech-savvy people: Don't click to investigate.** Not worth the risk.


**DON'T Call Numbers in the Text**


**Numbers in scam texts connect to scammers.**

- They impersonate customer service
- Trick you into providing information
- May charge expensive per-minute fees (international numbers)

**Look up official numbers yourself.**


**DON'T Give Information to "Verify" It's a Scam**


**Scammer: "For security, verify your account number."You: "Wait, is this a scam? Let me give you my number to check..."**


**Never provide information to verify whether something is a scam.** If you're unsure, it's a scam. Hang up or delete.


**DON'T Pay to "Cancel" or "Stop" Charges**


**Scam scenario:**

> "You've been charged $499 for McAfee antivirus. If you didn't authorize this, call 888-xxx-xxxx to cancel."

You call, they say: "To cancel, we need your bank info" OR "Pay $50 cancellation fee."


**This entire scenario is the scam.**

- No actual charge occurred
- They want you to provide bank info or pay fake fee
- Ignore completely

**Check actual bank/credit card statement** (not email or text claims).


**DON'T Feel Ashamed If You've Fallen for a Scam**


**Scams work because they're sophisticated and psychologically manipulative.**

- Targeting fear, urgency, authority, trust
- Designed by professionals to bypass critical thinking
- Smart, educated people fall for scams

**If scammed:**

- Act immediately (next section covers this)
- Report it
- Learn from it
- Don't let shame prevent you from protecting yourself going forward

## Step 5: What to Do If You Fell for a Scam


**If you clicked a link, provided information, or sent money:**


**Immediate Actions (Within First Hour):**


**If you provided financial information:**


**Credit/debit card number given:**

1. Call bank immediately (number on back of card)
2. Report card compromised
3. Request new card with new number
4. Dispute any fraudulent charges
5. Monitor account closely for 30 days

**Bank account info given:**

1. Call bank immediately
2. Explain account number may be compromised
3. Monitor account daily
4. Consider closing account and opening new one (if significant risk)

**Social Security Number given:**

1. Place fraud alert on credit reports:
    - Call one bureau (Equifax, Experian, or TransUnion)
    - They notify the other two
    - Requires verification before new credit opened in your name
2. File report at IdentityTheft.gov
3. Monitor credit reports closely (free at annualcreditreport.com)

**Passwords given:**

1. Change passwords immediately on affected accounts
2. Change passwords on any accounts using the same password
3. Enable two-factor authentication on all accounts
4. Check account activity for unauthorized access

**If you clicked a malicious link:**


**Mobile phone:**

1. Disconnect from WiFi and cellular (airplane mode)
2. Run security scan:
    - iPhone: Update iOS to latest version (Settings → General → Software Update)
    - Android: Install reputable antivirus (Malwarebytes, Norton Mobile Security)
    - Run full scan
3. Delete suspicious apps you don't recognize
4. Change passwords on important accounts (from different device if possible)
5. Contact mobile carrier to report (they may have additional protections)

**Computer:**

1. Disconnect from internet
2. Run antivirus scan (Windows Defender, Malwarebytes, etc.)
3. Change all passwords from clean device
4. Monitor for unusual activity

**If you sent money:**


**Gift cards:**

- Contact gift card company immediately (Google, Apple, Amazon, etc.)
- Provide card numbers if you have them
- They may freeze funds (unlikely but worth trying)
- Gift cards are rarely recoverable (scammers redeem quickly)

**Wire transfer (Western Union, MoneyGram):**

- Contact company immediately (within minutes, if possible)
- Report fraudulent transfer
- Request reversal (possible if not yet picked up)
- File fraud report

**Cryptocurrency:**

- Contact platform (Coinbase, etc.)
- Report transaction
- Cryptocurrency nearly impossible to reverse
- File police report

**Zelle, Venmo, CashApp:**

- Contact app support immediately
- Request reversal (difficult—these are designed for trusted transfers)
- File fraud report with bank (these connect to bank accounts)

**Check or money order:**

- Contact bank immediately
- Request stop payment (costs $30-35 but prevents cashing)
- Only works if check hasn't been cashed yet

**Follow-Up Actions (First Week):**


**File reports:**

1. **FTC:** IdentityTheft.gov or reportfraud.ftc.gov
    - Creates official identity theft report
    - Helps dispute fraudulent charges
    - Assists in recovering stolen identity
2. **FBI IC3:** ic3.gov (Internet Crime Complaint Center)
    - For significant financial losses
    - Helps law enforcement track trends
3. **Local police:**
    - File report in person
    - Get case number
    - Useful for disputing charges and identity theft recovery
4. **State Attorney General:** Most states have consumer protection divisions

**Monitor your accounts:**

- Check bank/credit card accounts daily for 30 days
- Check credit reports (annualcreditreport.com—free)
- Watch for unfamiliar accounts opened in your name

**Place fraud alert or credit freeze:**


**Fraud alert** (free):

- Requires creditors to verify identity before opening new accounts
- Lasts 1 year (renewable)
- Call one credit bureau: Equifax (888-766-0008), Experian (888-397-3742), or TransUnion (800-680-7289)
- They notify the other two

**Credit freeze** (free, stronger protection):

- Completely locks credit file—no new accounts can be opened
- Freeze at all three bureaus:
    - Equifax: equifax.com/personal/credit-report-services
    - Experian: experian.com/freeze/center
    - TransUnion: transunion.com/credit-freeze
- Temporarily unfreeze when you apply for credit yourself

**Consider identity theft protection:**

- Paid services (LifeLock, Identity Guard) monitor credit and dark web
- Worth considering if significant information compromised
- OR monitor yourself for free (more work, but effective)

**Long-Term (Ongoing):**


**Change security habits:**

- Use unique passwords for each account
- Enable two-factor authentication everywhere possible
- Never click links in unsolicited texts
- Verify before providing information

**Educate yourself:**

- Learn from the experience
- Share with friends and family
- Help others avoid same scam

**Don't let shame prevent action.** The sooner you act, the less damage done. Scammers count on victims being too embarrassed to report.


## Step 6: Protecting Yourself Going Forward


**Proactive Protection:**


**Enable Spam Filtering on Phone:**


**iPhone:**

- Settings → Messages → Filter Unknown Senders (toggle ON)
- Moves messages from people not in contacts to separate list
- Reduces exposure to scam texts

**Android:**

- Messages app → Menu (⋮) → Settings → Spam protection (toggle ON)
- Automatically filters suspected spam

**Carrier-level spam blocking:**


**AT&T Call Protect:**

- Free app, blocks spam calls and texts
- Download from App Store or Google Play

**Verizon Call Filter:**

- Free version available
- Blocks suspected spam

**T-Mobile Scam Shield:**

- Free for T-Mobile customers
- Blocks scam calls and texts

**Enable these at carrier level—very effective.**


**Register with National Do Not Call Registry:**

- donotcall.gov
- Reduces legitimate marketing (doesn't stop scammers, but reduces overall volume)

**Be Cautious Where You Share Your Number:**


**Limit sharing:**

- Don't post phone number on social media
- Use email for online forms when possible
- Consider using Google Voice number for non-essential services (free secondary number)

**Review social media privacy:**

- Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram: Make phone number private (not visible to public)
- Settings → Privacy → Who can see phone number → Only me

**Use Two-Factor Authentication (Prevents Account Takeover):**


**Enable 2FA on all important accounts:**

- Email (Gmail, Outlook, etc.)
- Banking and financial accounts
- Social media
- Shopping accounts (Amazon, etc.)

**Authenticator app (most secure):**

- Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator (free)
- More secure than SMS codes (scammers can intercept SMS)

**Be Skeptical by Default:**


**Healthy mindset:**

- Assume unsolicited texts are scams until proven otherwise
- Legitimate companies don't create urgency via text
- "If it seems suspicious, it is suspicious"
- It's okay to ignore texts you don't understand—nothing bad happens from ignoring scam texts

**Verify Everything:**

- Before clicking, before calling, before providing information
- Go to official sources (apps, websites, known phone numbers)
- Never trust contact information provided in suspicious text

**Educate Family Members:**


**Especially protect:**


**Elderly relatives:**

- Often targeted (perceived as less tech-savvy)
- May not recognize scam tactics
- Teach them to verify before acting

**Children and teens:**

- Less experience with scams
- May fall for prize/gaming scams
- Teach skepticism and verification

**Share this guide** with people you care about.


**Keep Software Updated:**


**Phone and computer:**

- Latest OS versions include security improvements
- Update when prompted
- Settings → Software Update (check for updates)

**Apps:**

- Keep banking apps, messaging apps updated
- Updates often include security patches

**Use Strong, Unique Passwords:**


**Password manager** (Bitwarden, 1Password, LastPass):

- Generates and stores strong passwords
- Different password for each account
- If one account breached, others remain safe

**Never reuse passwords** between important accounts (email, banking, etc.).


## Step 7: Special Situations


**Two-Factor Authentication Code Phishing:**


**New scam targeting 2FA:**

1. Scammer has your email/username (from data breach)
2. Scammer tries to log into your account → Triggers 2FA code sent to you
3. You receive legitimate 2FA code (from actual company)
4. Seconds later, scammer texts: "Your verification code is 482901. Reply if you didn't request this."
5. You reply with code, thinking you're reporting unauthorized attempt
6. Scammer now has your 2FA code → Logs into your account

**Red flags:**

- You receive 2FA code you didn't request
- Immediately followed by text asking you to confirm or deny the code

**Correct action:**

- Don't reply to any text about the code
- Change your password immediately (someone is trying to access your account)
- Enable 2FA via authenticator app (more secure than SMS)

**Business Email Compromise (Pretending to Be Your Boss):**


**If you receive text from "boss" asking for unusual favor:**


"Hey, I'm in a meeting. Can you buy $500 in gift cards and text me the codes? I'll reimburse you."


**Red flags:**

- Unusual request (boss never asks this)
- Gift cards (major red flag)
- Urgency
- Text instead of usual communication method

**Correct action:**

- Call boss on known number (or walk to their office)
- Verify request in person
- Don't comply without verification

**Scammers impersonate bosses, coworkers, IT departments.**


**QR Code Scams:**


**Scammers send texts with QR codes:**

> "Scan this QR code to verify your account."

**Risks:**

- QR code can link to malicious website
- Can trigger automatic payment
- Can install malware

**Correct action:**

- Don't scan QR codes from unsolicited texts
- Legitimate companies don't send important QR codes via text

**Voicemail Notification Scams:**


**Text claims you have new voicemail:**

> "You have 1 new voicemail. Listen here: [link]"

**Red flags:**

- Real voicemail notifications come through phone's built-in system
- Link goes to random website (not your carrier)

**Correct action:**

- Check voicemail through phone app or dialing voicemail
- Ignore text notification

**Delivery "Fee" Scams:**


**Text claims small fee to release package:**

> "Your package is held. Pay $2.95 redelivery fee: [link]"

**Why it works:**

- $2.95 seems legitimate and small
- You're not paying the fee—you're giving card number to scammers

**Once you enter card info, they have full number + CVV + expiration.**


**Real carriers:**

- Bill shippers, not recipients
- Don't demand fees via text link
- Use official billing systems

## Quick Reference: Scam or Legitimate?


**Use this checklist when you receive uncertain text:**


| Check              | Scam if...                                                         | Legitimate if...                                                 |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Contact**        | Unsolicited, unexpected                                            | You initiated contact or were expecting text                     |
| **Urgency**        | "Immediate action," "24 hours," threatens consequences             | Gives reasonable time, no threats                                |
| **Info requested** | Asks for SSN, passwords, account numbers, payment                  | Doesn't ask for sensitive info via text                          |
| **Link**           | Shortened link, misspelled domain, suspicious URL                  | Official domain or no link (tells you to visit website yourself) |
| **Greeting**       | "Dear customer," "Valued user," generic                            | Uses your actual name                                            |
| **Language**       | Grammar errors, awkward phrasing, excessive punctuation!!!         | Professional, clear, error-free                                  |
| **Payment method** | Gift cards, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, Zelle for stranger      | Credit card on official website, check to official address       |
| **Offer**          | Free prize, too good to be true                                    | Realistic, no "free money"                                       |
| **Sender**         | Random number, international number, doesn't match claimed company | Official short code, recognized number, matches company          |
| **Verification**   | Can't verify independently, company denies sending it              | Verified via official app, website, or phone number              |


**General rule: If 2+ red flags present = definitely scam. If 1 red flag + you're uncertain = treat as scam.**

## Conclusion


You've learned:


✅ What text message scams are and why they work (psychology, scale, tactics)
✅ Universal red flags that appear in ALL scams (urgency, suspicious links, requests for personal info, too good to be true)
✅ Specific scam categories (package delivery, banking, government, prizes, tech support, family emergency, romance)
✅ Exactly what to do when you receive suspicious text (don't click, don't reply, verify independently, delete, report)
✅ What NOT to do (don't reply "STOP," don't click "just to see," don't call numbers in text)
✅ What to do if you fell for a scam (immediate actions, reporting, monitoring, recovery)
✅ How to protect yourself going forward (spam filtering, 2FA, skepticism, education)
✅ Special situations (2FA code phishing, QR codes, voicemail scams)


**Key Principles:**


**Scammers rely on urgency:** They want you to react before thinking. The antidote: Pause. Slow down. Verify. Nothing legitimate requires instant response.


**Legitimate companies don't text sensitive requests:** Banks don't text asking for passwords. Government doesn't text demanding payments. Amazon doesn't text requesting account verification. If they did, they'd tell you to visit official website or call official number—not click a link.


**Links are the trap:** The entire scam hinges on you clicking the link. Don't click links in unsolicited texts. Ever. No exceptions. Even "just to see."


**Your number being targeted isn't personal:** Data breaches and random generation mean everyone's number eventually gets scammed. It's not because you're particularly vulnerable—it's because scammers send billions of texts hoping a tiny percentage respond.


**Shame helps scammers:** Embarrassment prevents victims from reporting and getting help. Scams are sophisticated, designed by professionals to exploit psychology. Smart people fall for them. Don't let shame prevent you from protecting yourself.


**Verification is everything:** Before clicking, calling, or providing information—verify independently. Visit official website, call official number, open official app. The 30 seconds this takes prevents hours or months of dealing with fraud.


**Your Action Plan:**


**Right now:**

- [ ] Enable spam filtering on your phone (Settings → Messages → Filter Unknown Senders or Spam protection)
- [ ] Save this number in contacts: **7726 (SPAM)** for reporting scam texts
- [ ] Review last few texts you received—any seem suspicious in hindsight?

**This week:**

- [ ] Enable two-factor authentication on email and banking (most important)
- [ ] Review social media privacy settings (hide phone number from public)
- [ ] Tell one family member about text scams (especially elderly relatives or young adults)

**Ongoing habit:**

- [ ] Before clicking any link in text: Pause and verify
- [ ] When receiving unexpected text: Assume scam until proven otherwise
- [ ] Delete and report suspicious texts (forward to 7726)
- [ ] Share this knowledge—help protect your community

**The best defense against scams is knowledge.** You now have it. Scammers depend on people not knowing these red flags, not verifying, not pausing to think. By reading this guide, you've armed yourself against the vast majority of text message scams.


**Trust your instincts. If it feels off, it is off. Slow down. Verify. Protect yourself.** 📱🛡️
